Here is a changelog:
# What's new in TensorFold

Each release's page on GitHub has its notes and measurements. See [the 1.0.0 release notes](RELEASE-NOTES-1.0.0.md) for the native binary's supported models and migration details.

## 1.0.9

- `tensorfold pull` finishes into a relative cache root (a relative `HF_HUB_CACHE` or `HF_HOME`), and `pull --exlr8` into a relative `--dir`. The shipped binary stopped at the first finished file with an assertion failure, because it moved files with a call that only takes absolute paths. The checkpoint CLI's tests now run with the safety checks the binary ships with, and a new test fetches an EXLR8 node's small and large files into a relative folder (#700). Thanks to @chaog992.
- The Flash Next recipe names the checkpoint the native engine serves on Macs, `TensorFold/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MLX-6bit-MTP`, with `--temperature 0`, says the 4-bit checkpoint is refused at load, and marks its other sections as the Python 0.6.6 engine's (#705). Thanks to @cwschroeder.
- The native CUDA host forwards every entry a family's lane backend gives it. It dropped `prefill_step`, `prepare_features` and `features`, so the lane core saw a backend that cannot run a prompt a chunk at a time: a CUDA family that can would have run every prompt whole, with other streams' decode waiting for all of it. No CUDA family in this release runs its prompt in chunks yet, so replies are unchanged, and a test now fails when a backend entry is added without being forwarded. In the author's runs of a GLM-5.3-Flash port on two GB10s that does (#548), a decode beside a fresh 32k-token prompt waited at most 1.7 s between tokens instead of 27.9 s (#742). Thanks to @Bizuayeu.
- The prompt cache keeps a state that several continuations resume, such as a turn sent again, a regenerated or edited reply, or an agent that starts each step from the same history. Once one continuation had kept its own longer state, the cache counted that history as superseded and freed it first when a later prompt needed room, so every later continuation read the whole history again and kept nothing there either. A state resumed again after a longer prompt kept a state extending it is now a branch point, freed only as the least recently used, while a conversation that only grows still frees its old turns first. The paged store takes the same rule. Replies are unchanged, since only the choice of which state to free changes. Served with Nemotron and a small cache (0.3 GiB on an M3 Ultra, 1 GiB on a GB10), two forks of a 3,962-token conversation each kept a longer state, and unrelated prompts followed until the cache had to free one: a third fork then resumed the history's 3,956 tokens, where 1.0.8 had freed the history and read it all again. A conversation that only grows resumed the previous turn's prompt every turn with and without the change, and every reply equalled the cache-off server's (#735). Thanks to @BadAd84.
- Nemotron's GPU samplers on Metal and CUDA read one sampling rule, built once from the request: 1 / T, top_p, the candidates' near window, ln(min_p), top_k and the seed. Before, Metal's host, CUDA's sampler and the CUDA tests each built their own copy of the same values. The kernels and their arguments are unchanged, so sampled replies are the same tokens, and host tests pin the Metal cfg row and the CUDA rule's layout. On an M3 Ultra and a GB10, Nemotron's seeded sampled replies to 8 prompts, and 12 more cells across temperature, top_p, top_k (0 to 3,000) and min_p, were the same tokens before and after, drafted and with `"draft": false` (#731). Thanks to @jschmied.
- CUDA has shared row kernels for every family: RMS norm rows, the residual add with its norm, a bf16 residual stream's add and norm with the 64-value group sums a 4-bit projection reads, gated head norms, and token rows from a 4-bit (MLX layout) or bf16 embedding table. Each has a float64 reference, and `tf-cuda-test norms` and `norm-rows` check them against it and check that every row count gives the widest run's bits. Nemotron's 4-bit token rows now run on the shared kernel when it serves with our own kernels rather than a captured Triton set, with the same bits as its own kernel, which is gone. A captured set keeps its own token rows, and Nemotron keeps its own norm kernels, whose sums run in another order; no family uses the shared norms yet. On a GB10, Nemotron's replies with our own kernels were the same tokens before and after, drafted and with `"draft": false`, and decode and cold prefill (2k to 32k tokens) were within 1% (#736). Thanks to @jschmied.
- FP8 (e4m3) and NVFP4 (e2m1 codes with e4m3 scales every 16 inputs) values and their float64 references live in one place on the host, `fp8.zig` and `nvfp4.zig` beside the other formats in `core/quant`. The CUDA tests and `tensorfold check-precision` decode through them instead of keeping three copies of the same arithmetic, which is unchanged, so no kernel and no reply changes. A reference refuses what it cannot read: a scale type other than fp32, bf16 or fp16, an empty projection, or an expert stack whose scales or global scales don't match its weights. Host tests check that every finite e4m3 code rounds to itself, that ties go to even and large values stop at 448, and FP8 and NVFP4 expert stacks against values decoded by hand. On a GB10, every kernel and the CUDA server built byte-identical with and without the change, and `tf-cuda-test quant-ref` and `modelopt` printed the same output, byte for byte (#730). The host now reads e4m3's two NaN codes, 0x7f and 0xff, as NaN, as the GPU's conversion does, where it read them as ±480; no checkpoint holds them. Thanks to @jschmied.
- `tf-metal-counters` (`zig build tf-metal-counters`) times GPU work on a Mac with the GPU's own counters and no model: three dependent FP32 operators, each timed between counter samples at its encoder's start and end, with GPU ticks turned into seconds from two readings of the CPU and GPU clocks rather than from CPU time. It checks the outputs against values computed independently and against an untimed run, bit for bit, and refuses to read, reset or free its samples while their command buffer runs. A GPU without the counters it needs is reported as unsupported, with no CPU timing in their place. On an M3 Ultra and an M5 Ultra, sampling at encoder boundaries works and sampling at dispatch boundaries is not supported, which the probe reports. No engine uses it: the Mac server built with and without it has the same code and data, byte for byte (#680, #676). Thanks to @akol1.
- The fragment check Nemotron and Flash Next run at every load on a Mac, which proves on the GPU that `nax.h`'s matrix fragments give the host's sums, now catches a transposed operand. Its test values, `(i * 7 + salt * 3) mod 5`, made every block of the transposed operand symmetric (its row pitch, 16, is 1 mod 5), so loading it as a plain one gave the same sums; values mod 13 leave no such block and keep every sum an exact small integer. A new GPU test runs the check and, before M5, the same check with the transposed load swapped for a plain one, which must fail. On M5 the multiply does the transpose, so there the test checks the layout alone. On an M3 Ultra the new test passes, and fails with the old values put back. Replies are unchanged (#744). Thanks to @harrisonfriia.
- GLM-5.3-Flash on a Mac runs that fragment check at every load too, right after its kernels compile, as Nemotron and Flash Next do: its prompt kernels and decode attention read the same fragments, so a GPU whose layout gives wrong sums now stops the load with `error.FragLayout` instead of serving wrong tokens. A load that passes adds one small dispatch. On an M3 Ultra with 8 of the 45 layers, a build whose check was made to fail stopped at load, and the real build's replies were the same tokens as before, drafted and with `"draft": false`, decode and cold prefill (2k to 32k tokens) were within 0.2%, and a warm load took 5.1 s on both builds (#745). Thanks to @harrisonfriia.
- The 27B on a Mac no longer copies each DeltaNet layer's recurrent state after a chain round. A plain decode step, a verified draft chain and a prompt chunk scanned each of the 48 DeltaNet layers' states (3 MiB of fp32 per stream) into a second buffer and then copied it back: about 288 MiB read and written for every decoded token, in one more dependent dispatch per layer. When a round's rows keep their slots, the scan now runs on the state where it is and only the convolution history is copied; a round whose slots move keeps the copy. The scan does the same arithmetic on the same inputs, so every output bit is unchanged (#711). Thanks to @jkuepker.
- The 27B's decode attention on an M5 runs fewer dependent dispatches. A chain of decode rows, as in a plain step or a verified draft chain, now attends to its own keys in the prefix kernel, so the tail kernel, its query repack and the gate dispatch go away: a one-row step runs 4 dispatches with 3 barriers in each of the 16 attention layers instead of 7 with 5. The tree-round merge loads its chunk partials ahead and applies the query gate itself with the same bf16 rounding, rows past a stream's last query are no longer written, and each tile's two head-dim halves run on their own simdgroups. Chunk partials, tile boundaries and merge order are the tail kernel's, so every output byte is the same; a round with a branching row, a stream that is not a chain, or a GPU without tensor units keeps the tail kernel. `tf-qwen27-attention-fused` also checks plans without a shared prefix, 5 to 8 streams and 16-row windows (#712). Thanks to @jkuepker.
- The 27B's DFlash2 drafts on a Mac wait less. The drafter's first command buffer starts after 6 operations instead of 40, its row copies go out as one dispatch, shared-context attention loads four keys before it folds them (in key order, with the same fp32 sums), and wide bf16 top-k rows are split over sixteen threadgroups. In the check tools' run path, a drafted round's cache and state commit also runs behind the next draft; the server still finishes it at once. Tokens, rounds and accepted drafts are unchanged. With #711 and #712, on an M5 Ultra (four runs a build, 256 tokens, one stream), greedy decode went from 406.1 to 417.0 tok/s on code and from 100.6 to 103.6 on prose, and seeded sampling from 294.0 to 316.9 on code and from 86.2 to 89.0 on prose; on an M3 Ultra (six runs), greedy code went from 150.6 to 154.7 and prose from 53.3 to 54.8. Prompt processing at 16k, 32k and 64k tokens on the M3 Ultra was 0.2 to 0.4% faster. Replies were the same tokens drafted and with `"draft": false`, on both builds, resumed and fresh, and concurrent and alone (#713). Thanks to @jkuepker.
- The Metal EXL3 projection reads each 16-bit trellis state without a branch: a shift and a masked carry from the next word give the same 16 bits as the old two-way window at every offset, 0 to 31, so the hoisted kernel's states, weights and outputs keep #681's bits. A new GPU test checks the window against the host's value for 35,040 pattern and offset pairs, and the existing fixtures still match (#718). Thanks to @mrv777.
- GLM-5.3-Flash's sparse attention runs on an M1. Its generated kernels (64 and 32 heads) now declare the 1,024 threads their caller launches; an M1 Max compiled them for 832, so the launch left their outputs at zero. Kernel bodies, dispatch sizes and tolerances are unchanged, and the regression tests now also check the pipeline's capacity and compare both kernels against an independent float64 reference (#704). Thanks to @mrv777.
- Living Weights trains Nemotron on an M1. `tf_train_ssm_back` now declares the 1,024 threads training launches per head; an M1 Max compiled it for 768, which could leave gradients unwritten with no command-buffer error. Arithmetic and dispatch sizes are unchanged, and new GPU tests check gradients, seeded checkpoints, shared groups and checkpoint boundaries, the production 64-head, 8-group shape included, against float64 and finite differences (#715). Thanks to @mrv777.
- Nemotron on CUDA runs a prompt in passes of up to 4,096 rows instead of 2,048-row chunks, so each pass reads the routed experts' weights once for twice as many rows. A row's bits do not depend on where a pass is cut, so replies and kept prompt states are unchanged; staggered segments, layer dumps, lessons and a pass that would hold more prompt-cache marks than the scan arms at once (16) keep 2,048-row chunks, and the startup line says "prompts in passes of up to 4096 rows". On a GB10 with Nemotron 3.5 Lightning (MLX 4-bit), cold prompts of 8k, 16k, 32k and 64k tokens prefill 7.2%, 6.8%, 6.3% and 5.4% faster, and 2k as before (#720). Thanks to @plotarmordev.
- `tf-cuda-test prompt-cuts` checks Nemotron's CUDA prompt states against one uncut pass: a pass that keeps states inside chunks and at their ends, then a pass resumed from every keep with the key and value rows past it filled first, comparing the states, the MTP head's caches, the last hidden row, the logits and the first token. The checks come from #721 and #722, whose changes 1.0.8 had already made in its own form, and on a GB10 they pass at 3,073, 4,096, 4,097 and 8,193 tokens on the MLX 4-bit and NVFP4 checkpoints. Thanks to @plotarmordev.
- Nemotron on CUDA prefills each reply in the background for the next turn when the prompt cache is on, as the Mac engines do: after a reply, the conversation through it and the next turn's opening run as a background pass that steps aside at its next chunk for a foreground request, so the next turn resumes after the reply instead of reading it again. On a GB10, a second turn resumed 7,366 of its 7,389 prompt tokens where the build before it resumed 7,228. When the next request arrives before the background pass has run, the pass steps aside and keeps nothing, so that turn resumes from an older state: in the same chat, a regenerated third turn resumed 7,366 tokens where the build before it resumed 7,540 (#723). Thanks to @plotarmordev.
- Nemotron on CUDA no longer makes a request wait for the background pass that prefills a reply for its chat's next turn. The pass starts only once the engine has had no other work for 150 ms, so a request sent the moment a reply ends goes first, and the pass is dropped before it reaches the GPU. On a MoE every prompt chunk reads most of the experts' weights, so even a 20-row pass held a GB10 for about 45 ms. A pass that is running steps aside after its current chunk, now at most 256 rows, and keeps the state it reached. Since a pass may not run at all, each turn keeps its own history state again, as in 1.0.8, so back-to-back and regenerated turns resume as they did there. Replies are unchanged. On a GB10 with Nemotron 3.5 Lightning (MLX 4-bit), a new chat's ~1,000-token first turn sent right after another reply started after 0.199 s, as in 1.0.8 (0.200 s) where the first merge of the background pass took 0.240 s, and longer ones kept #720's gain: 6% sooner than 1.0.8 at ~10k tokens and 7% at ~20k. In chats with a second between turns, later turns resumed past each reply and started 2.0-2.2x sooner than in 1.0.8.
- Nemotron on CUDA times the draft-depth rule's window costs on the window a drafted round verifies: the pending token at the prompt's end, the MTP head drafting first as in a round, then the text's own next tokens as the window's drafts. 1.0.8 advanced a token before timing. The window's drafts are never the head's own chain, which loops past its confident levels (" the river bank, the river was still the same river"): rows that repeat a token share experts, and such windows read 7-10% under what decoding pays at 8 to 11 rows. Replies are unchanged. On a GB10 the table's shape is within 2.8% of what decoding pays, and over 16 prompts the mean decode speed is within 0.4% of 1.0.8's table for code and prose, greedy and sampled.
- `/v1/responses` accepts OpenAI's `include` values (such as `reasoning.encrypted_content` or `message.output_text.logprobs`) and ignores them, where it used to refuse any `include`, so clients that always send it can call the server. A value that is not one of OpenAI's names is still refused (#759). Thanks to @Bizuayeu.
- GLM tool calls that the model wrote slightly wrong still parse: an argument key written without its `<arg_key>` gets it back, and a call the end token cut off inside its value is closed when the closed call then parses strictly. A key with no value, a tool not offered, or text after an argument still stays as reply text. The repairs and their cases come from @MiaAI-Lab's #285 (#761). Thanks to @Bizuayeu and @MiaAI-Lab.
- The native server's tokenizer keeps the ids of long text pieces between added tokens (up to 64 MiB), so a chat's earlier messages are not tokenized again: each request renders its chat up to three times, and every turn sends the earlier messages back. Encoding gives the same ids. On a GB10 with Nemotron, the server's time before the prompt pass on a later turn fell from 12.6 to 1.6 ms at 12k tokens and from 41.5 to 2.3 ms at 35k, with every reply the same. Every family the native server serves goes through this tokenizer. On a GB10 and an M3 Ultra, `/tokenize` gives the same ids as the build before it for every turn of two five-turn chats and for three long documents (Nemotron on both, Qwen3.8-27B on the Mac), and the tokenizers of Nemotron, Qwen3.8-27B, Qwen3.5-2B, Flash Next and GLM-5.3 give a fresh encode's ids through the memo; the tokenizer's own tests now run in `test-cuda-host` (#767). Thanks to @plotarmordev.
- Nemotron on CUDA drafts every stream of a shared round in one batch: each head level runs one forward with a row per stream still drafting, where each stream's head used to run its levels one row at a time. Drafts and their confidences equal the one-at-a-time ones to the bit, greedy and sampled, so replies are unchanged. On a GB10 with distinct prompts, 400-token replies finish 5% sooner at 2 streams, 7% at 4 and 10% at 8 (315 against 282 tok/s); a lone stream is unchanged. A batched head runs with a captured Triton set too: it normalizes the streams' last rows in one launch on aligned rows, as that set needs. A build that drafted each batched stream again alone found no draft id or confidence that differed in 4,300 rounds and 34,460 levels (MLX 4-bit with our kernels and with the captured set, and NVFP4). Together with #769, #770 and #771, on a GB10 (MLX 4-bit, distinct prompts, 256-token replies) aggregate decode rose 4.4-5.5% at 2 streams, 9.4-11.6% at 4 and 11.8-14.7% at 8 over the build before them, every reply equal to its solo run (#768). Thanks to @plotarmordev.
- A shared round prices each stream's drafts by the head steps they take, apart from the round's own overhead, and a head that drafts every stream in one batch costs the deepest stream's steps. The overhead learned before also held the steps of the depths it was measured at, so it kept the depths it saw. On a GB10 with Nemotron's batched heads and distinct prompts, 4 streams finish 3.3% to 3.5% sooner across three sessions and 2, 3 and 6 streams 0.6% to 2.6%, with the same replies; 8 streams are unchanged. A family whose head drafts one stream at a time pays a head step a draft: on an M3 Ultra, Nemotron's shared rounds at 2, 4 and 8 streams measured within 3% of the build before it either way (a mean of +0.8%) with the same replies, and the 27B, whose budgets carry no head steps, within 1% (#769). Thanks to @plotarmordev.
- Nemotron on CUDA runs a shared round's per-stream steps for all its streams at once: each Mamba layer's conv and scan, and each attention layer's key write, chunks and merge, take one launch for every stream instead of one per stream, each stream still on its own state, caches and position. Every stream's rows equal its one-at-a-time ones to the bit, so replies are unchanged. On a GB10 with distinct prompts, 400-token replies finish 5% to 8% sooner at 8 streams and 3% at 4 across sessions; one and two streams are unchanged. `tf-cuda-test glue` compares the shared-window kernels with the one-stream ones byte for byte, for eight conv and scan shapes and eight attention shapes in every slot of eight streams and in two- and three-stream windows (#770). Thanks to @plotarmordev.
- Nemotron on CUDA keeps more of each decode step's loads in flight: the MoE sum loads a row's eight slot values before adding them, the Mamba scan loads every step's inputs before its steps, and an attention window of several rows loads its next key tile while it computes the current one. The values and the order of every sum are unchanged, so replies are unchanged. On a GB10, one 400-token reply decodes 2% faster, and at 56k and 112k tokens of context 3% and 5% faster. On a GB10 with MLX 4-bit, a lone stream decoded 1.9% to 2.4% faster over eight prompts, greedy and sampled, on a shared window-cost table and on each build's own, and cold prompts of 2k to 64k tokens prefill as before (within 0.7%). `tf-cuda-test glue` now checks one-row windows as well, which keep the plain chunk kernel (#771). Thanks to @plotarmordev.
- Qwen3.8-27B serves on Apple's GPU generation 18 (M6). A Mac mini M6 (12-core GPU, 32 GB) ran the 27B with its DFlash2 drafter on 1.0.8 with this one change: drafted replies equal to `"draft": false` byte for byte at 16k and 32k contexts, thinking budgets cut where asked, long-context recall, no swap, and the same reply hashes as earlier builds on that Mac. Later generations still refuse until someone runs them (#643). Thanks to @RS91Dev.
- The 27B and Flash Next on a Mac keep a prompt state inside prompts under 4,096 tokens, where they kept none: the history's mark, at the last chunk end the prompt pass cuts anyway, so it adds no prompt call. A repeated first turn now resumes, and so does a follow-up with thinking on, whose reply state never prefixes the next turn because the template drops the reasoning. On an M3 Ultra at the default cache budget, a 27B follow-up of about 2,900 tokens with thinking on starts in 0.4-0.5 s instead of 10.4-10.6 s, and a repeated 1,600-token first turn in 0.18 s instead of 5.5 s; on an M5 Ultra, Flash Next's follow-ups of 1,000-3,000 tokens start in 0.08-0.10 s instead of 0.35-0.82 s. Replies are byte for byte the same, and first turns take under 0.5% longer. A short prompt's mark inside its request's shared system block is kept as the block's state, so the request's own reply state no longer evicts it first.
- On a Mac, a Nemotron MoE layer that Living Weights taught runs its pocket as two dispatches beside other work, where it ran three after the shared expert, each behind a barrier: `tf_pocket_in` (the dot product and squared relu in one kernel, adding in the old kernel's order) runs beside the router and the shared expert's up projection, and the pocket's output beside the routed experts' down projection. Each sum keeps its order, so replies are unchanged. On an M5 Max, `tf_pocket_in` takes 4.6 to 5.6 us a call, under the 21 us of the up projection beside it. On an M3 Ultra, a folder taught two facts gave the same replies token for token, drafted and with `"draft": false`, and decoded 8.2% faster greedy and 8.3% sampled over eight prompts; the kernel test is byte-equal there too (#775). Thanks to @ThinkOffApp.
- `prompt_logprobs` on CUDA reads its prompt rows through the head 256 rows a pass instead of 16, so the head's weights are read once for every 256 rows, into a logits buffer of its own (64 MiB, made at the first such request; without the memory it keeps 16-row passes). The rows are unchanged to the bit. On a GB10, the extra cost of `prompt_logprobs` on an 8,741-token prompt fell from 0.70 s to 0.13 s (2.03 s to 1.46 s in all at 0 alternatives, 2.53 s to 1.79 s at 20), and on a 3,377-token prompt from 0.27 s to 0.05 s. On a GB10 the rows were byte-equal to the 16-row passes at 300, 3,377, 4,097 and 8,741 tokens with 0 and 20 alternatives, on MLX 4-bit (our kernels and the captured set) and NVFP4. Over four servers a build (MLX 4-bit), the extra time at 8,741 tokens fell from 0.71 s to 0.12 s at 0 alternatives and from 1.21 s to 0.47 s at 20, and at 3,377 tokens from 0.29 s to 0.06 s. The buffer stays for the server's life once made (#776). Thanks to @plotarmordev.
- Nemotron on CUDA decodes a lone request that asks for `logprobs` on its lone driver, as it does requests without them: the driver commits each round's kept rows as the lane core's windows read them, so the rows and tokens are unchanged. On a GB10, a 400-token greedy reply with `logprobs` costs 0.3% more than one without at 0 alternatives, 0.9% at 5 and 3.1% at 20, against 4.6%, 5.6% and 8.4% before. On a GB10 (MLX 4-bit with our kernels and with the captured set, and NVFP4), the lone driver's rows and tokens equalled the lane core's byte for byte at 0, 5 and 20 alternatives, greedy and seeded sampled, with thinking on and off, streamed and not, and equalled `"draft": false`. Over four servers a build, a 400-token reply with `logprobs` cost 0.4%, 1.4% and 4.1% more than one without, against 4.6%, 5.6% and 8.9% before (#777). Thanks to @plotarmordev.
- Nemotron on CUDA decodes a lone request with a thinking budget above 32 tokens, or with `--loop-guard`, on its lone driver, which hands the stream to the lane core just before the budget's cut or a loop guard's close, so the close is forced as before and replies are unchanged. On a GB10, 700-token thinking replies with a 4,000-token budget finished 3.3% and 8.1% sooner, with a 400-token budget that cuts 3.6 to 4.2% sooner, and with `--loop-guard` 4% and 8% sooner. On a GB10 (MLX 4-bit and NVFP4), thinking budgets of 33, 48, 400, 1,000 and 4,000 tokens gave the lane core's replies token for token, greedy and seeded sampled, cut at the same token, and equalled `"draft": false`; the short budgets went to the lane core just before their cut and the long ones stayed on the lone driver to the end. With `--loop-guard`, prompts that make the reasoning repeat a token stopped at the same token with the same period as before (15 of 24 replies over the two formats), and every reply equalled the previous build's and `"draft": false`. Over four servers a build, 700-token thinking replies with a 4,000-token budget finished 6.3% and 8.7% sooner and one cut at 400 tokens 4.0% sooner (#778). Thanks to @plotarmordev.
- Nemotron on CUDA decodes a lone structured-output request (`response_format`, a required tool call) on its lone driver: each window's chain is cut and grown by the grammar and its rows masked as the lane core's are, so replies are unchanged. On a GB10, 500-token JSON replies finished 8% sooner under `json_object` and 13% under a JSON schema, and required tool calls 14% sooner. On a GB10 (MLX 4-bit with both kernel sets, and NVFP4), a JSON object, two JSON schemas, a regex, a choice, required and named tool calls, and a schema and a required call after a 300-token thinking budget all gave the lane core's replies token for token, greedy and seeded sampled, and equalled `"draft": false`. Over four servers a build, a 370-token `json_object` reply finished 4% to 7% sooner and a required tool call 15% sooner (#779). Thanks to @plotarmordev.
- Nemotron on CUDA hands the lane core's last live stream back to its lone driver once the requests beside it finish and nothing waits: the driver resumes from the round the lane core drafted, so replies are unchanged. On a GB10, an 800-token greedy reply started beside a short one finished about 5% sooner; seeded sampled replies were unchanged. Only a lone driver that resumes a stream gets one back: on a Mac, Nemotron's and the 27B's lone drivers open every stream they are given, so a stream the lane core holds stays there to its end, as before. On a GB10 (MLX 4-bit with both kernel sets, and NVFP4), replies started beside a short one equalled their runs alone, greedy and seeded sampled, with `logprobs`, a JSON object and a thinking budget too, and 2, 4 and 8 concurrent requests equalled their solo runs; over four servers a build, an 800-token reply beside a 10-token one finished 1% to 2% sooner. On an M3 Ultra, Nemotron and the 27B kept concurrent replies equal to solo at 2 and 4 streams (#780). Thanks to @plotarmordev.
- The 27B on a Mac builds its Neural Engine prompt share only when the share fits under the 70% load limit beside the loaded model. The share keeps an fp16 copy of 3,072 MLP columns of every layer, 5,760 MiB, outside the GPU's own count, and on a 32 GB Mac it took the server into swap for about 5% faster prompts (#643, reported by @RS91Dev). Such a Mac now runs prompts on the GPU alone and says so at load; with the 4-bit checkpoint, Macs with 48 GB or more keep the share.
- `--cortheon` puts Cortheon's reasoning program and web research inside the native server, for chat completions, `/v1/responses` and `/v1/messages`, with no change for clients. The model gets Cortheon's stages for its task type and two tools the server runs itself, `cortheon_search` (DuckDuckGo's HTML results, or Brave's API with `BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY`) and `cortheon_fetch`, whose calls the client never sees. A question about current or version-specific facts, or a request to build with an outside library or API, is researched before the model starts: the model writes up to three queries, and the server reads up to three of the best pages. A coding task that changed files after its last test is asked once to run it before finishing, and a researched answer without a URL is asked once for its sources. Web text loses sentences that read as orders to the model, and reads reach public addresses only, each redirect checked, pinned to the checked address, with TLS verified, 2 MiB and 15 seconds at most. The rounds a client never saw are kept and put back in front of their reply on the next turn, so the prompt cache resumes it. Without the flag every reply is unchanged.
